items.title: Petra's Lab Partner Says One Thing and Codes Another

scenario.gentle:
Petra is a junior in a college engineering lab, partnered with Marcus for a semester-long robotics project worth 30% of their grade. They are building an autonomous line-following robot, and the prototype demo is in eleven days. Petra has been handling the hardware assembly while Marcus owns the software. On Tuesday, she walks into the lab to find Marcus sitting in front of his laptop, the fluorescent lights buzzing overhead, the smell of solder from a neighboring bench drifting through the room. She asks about his progress.

Petra: 'Hey Marcus, where are we on the PID controller? I finished the sensor mount yesterday so we should be good to start integration testing this weekend.'

Marcus: 'Yeah, it is basically done. I just need to clean up a few functions and push it to the repo.'

Petra: 'Awesome. Can I pull the branch tonight and start testing the sensor readings against it?'

Marcus: 'Uh, maybe give me until Thursday. I want to make sure the edge cases are handled before you see it.'

Petra checks the shared repository that evening and finds that Marcus's last commit was nine days ago. The branch has 40 lines of boilerplate code and no PID logic at all. She pulls up the commit history on her phone, the screen glowing in her dark apartment, and realizes the gap between what Marcus said and what exists is not a matter of cleanup. The code is not close to done. It has not been started.

items.title: Naomi's Client Win and the Team Lead Who Wanted to Debrief

scenario.gentle:
Naomi closed the firm's largest deal in two years, a contract worth three times her annual target. Her team lead, Ivan, has been at the same level for four years without closing anything comparable. During the team meeting the next morning, Ivan called for a debrief. The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead as eight people settled into their chairs.

Ivan: 'Great work on the Meridian deal, Naomi. Really. I think it would be valuable for the team if we walked through your process so everyone can learn from it. How did you get them to sign at that price point?'

Naomi: 'Thanks, Ivan. Honestly, a lot of it came from the relationship-building phase. I spent three months just listening before I pitched anything.'

Ivan: 'Three months is a long runway, though. That is a lot of unbillable time. Did you flag that with leadership, or was it more of a gamble?'

Naomi paused. She could feel the framing shift from 'teach us' to 'justify yourself.'

Ivan: 'I just want to make sure we are documenting the full picture, not just the outcome. Process matters as much as results if we want this to be replicable.'

Naomi: 'That makes sense. I can put together a written breakdown for the team. Would that work?'

Ivan: 'Perfect. And maybe loop me in on the timeline details so I can help contextualize the resource investment for the partners.'

items.title: Tomás and His Brother Have the Conversation They Have Been Avoiding

scenario.gentle:
Tomas got promoted to director six months ago. His younger brother Marco has been at the same level at a different company for three years. They are in their parents' backyard on a Sunday. Tomas has been sending Marco unsolicited career advice for weeks: articles, book recommendations, a late-night text about title renegotiation.

Marco sets his drink down. 'Can I say something without you turning it into a coaching session?'

Tomas laughs. 'I do not coach you.'

'Nine articles in three weeks. A book about executive presence at 11 PM.'

'I am trying to help. I know what works.'

Marco pauses. 'You got one promotion. One. I have been doing this three years. I know my situation better than you do.'

Tomas opens his mouth, then stops. For the first time, he wonders if the advice was about helping Marco or confirming how far he has come.
scenario.direct:

At their parents' house on Sunday, Marco says: 'Can I say something without you turning it into a coaching session?'

Tomás: 'I do not coach you.'

Marco: 'Nine articles. A book about executive presence at 11 PM. You told me to renegotiate my title like it never occurred to me.'

Tomás: 'I have been through this. I know what moves the needle.'

Marco: 'You got one promotion. And you are acting like you have a system. I have been in my role for three years. You do not know my company, my manager, or my situation.'

Tomás goes quiet. He does not have a response that would not sound like more advice.

Tomás: 'Always.'

Marco: 'You sent me nine articles. Told me to renegotiate my title. Texted a book on executive presence at 11 PM.'

Marco: 'You got one promotion. One. I have been doing this for three years. You do not know my situation.'

Tomás stands there holding his drink. For the first time, it occurs to him the advice was not entirely about Marco.

items.title: Sage and Dex Disagree About Tempo in the Practice Room

scenario.gentle:
Sage and Dex are preparing for a duet performance at the conservatory's spring showcase. They have been rehearsing for three weeks in a small practice room with a piano, two stands, and a metronome that sits between them like a referee. The piece is a modern composition that shifts between fast, aggressive passages and slow, lyrical ones. Sage, a pianist, keeps pushing the tempo in the aggressive sections. Dex, a violinist, keeps pulling it back. They are standing on opposite sides of the piano with their scores open, and neither is smiling.

Dex spoke first: 'You are rushing the forte sections again. The composer marked those at 120. You are playing them at 140.'

Sage set her jaw. 'The marked tempo sounds flat. There is no energy at 120. The audience falls asleep.'

'The audience is not our concern right now,' Dex said, adjusting his chin rest. 'We have not mastered the phrasing at the correct tempo. If we cannot play it clean at 120, playing it sloppy at 140 does not help.'

Sage closed the fallboard over the keys. 'So we just play it safe? That is your plan for the showcase?'

Noor, their faculty advisor, had been listening from the doorway without either of them noticing. She stepped inside. 'Can I ask both of you something? Sage, what would happen to the piece if you played the lyrical sections with the same intensity you bring to the forte? And Dex, what would happen if you let the aggressive sections breathe a little instead of controlling every beat?'

Both of them were quiet for a moment. Sage opened the fallboard again. Dex repositioned his bow.

Noor walked in and cut through it: 'Sage, what if you brought your intensity to the lyrical sections? Dex, what if you let the aggressive parts breathe instead of locking them down?'

Silence. Then Sage opened the piano again.

items.title: Juno Watches Her Newsroom Turn a Rumor Into a Story

scenario.gentle:
Juno is a junior staff writer at her campus newspaper. The newsroom is small, eight desks pushed together in a basement office that smells like old coffee and printer ink. The editor-in-chief, Alma, has just walked in with a tip: a student government senator allegedly used student activity funds for a personal trip. No documents yet, just a text screenshot from an anonymous source. The room starts buzzing.

Alma: 'This is huge. If this holds up, it is front page.'

Knox, the sports editor who covers student government as a side beat, leans back in his chair: 'I have heard rumors about that senator for months. This tracks completely.'

Faye, the photo editor, pulls up the senator's Instagram: 'Look, she posted from Cabo two weeks ago. Who pays for Cabo on a student budget?'

Knox: 'Exactly. And I heard from someone in the budget committee that her expense reports were flagged last semester.'

Alma: 'Knox, can you confirm the expense report thing?' Knox shrugs: 'Not officially, but the source was solid.'

Juno has been quiet. She covered a student government budget hearing last month and knows that the senator's trip was actually funded by an outside scholarship she disclosed to the committee. The disclosure is in the public minutes Juno downloaded three weeks ago. She watches the room build a story on a foundation of secondhand claims and confirmation bias. Nobody has asked for the budget committee minutes.

Alma turns to the room: 'I want a draft by Thursday. Juno, you are on this with Knox.'

items.title: Ravi's Team Pushes Back on the Deadline

scenario.gentle:
Ravi leads a small product team at a health-tech company. The VP of engineering just moved the launch date up by three weeks, and Ravi has been told to make it happen. He calls a meeting with his four-person team. The energy in the room is already heavy.

Ravi started carefully. 'I want to be upfront with everyone. The launch date moved to March 14th. That is three weeks earlier than we planned. I know that is hard to hear.'

Sara, the senior developer, leaned back in her chair. 'Ravi, we already cut the testing window once. If we cut it again, we are shipping bugs to real patients. This is a health app. That is not something I am comfortable with.'

'I hear that,' Ravi said. 'And I want you to know I said the same thing to the VP this morning. He did not move.'

Devon, the junior designer, looked up from his notebook. 'So what are we supposed to do? Just work weekends until we burn out?'

Ravi paused for a moment before answering. 'No. Here is what I am proposing. We scope down the launch to the three core features that are already tested and push the rest to a 2.0 release in April. The VP gets his date. We do not ship untested code. Nobody works weekends. But I need to know if that feels workable to you, because I am not going to commit to it unless the team thinks it can hold.'

Sara looked at Devon. Devon looked at the whiteboard. After a few seconds, Sara said, 'That could work. But only if we get written confirmation that the 2.0 features are funded, not just promised.'

Ravi nodded. 'I will get that in writing before end of day Friday. If I cannot get it, we revisit this plan on Monday.'
